outcome: The twin prime conjecture itself remains open, but the associated bound H1 (the smallest gap between primes proven to recur infinitely often, equal to 2 iff the conjecture is true) moved dramatically in a rapid, contested sequence in late August/early September 2026: 246 (2014, pre-window) -> 240 (Julia Stadlmann, human, arXiv 31 Aug 2026) -> 236 (Shiva Kintali, AI-assisted, X announcement 1 Sep 2026, unreviewed, no preprint) -> 212 (Axiom Math's AxiomProver AI system, ~2-3 Sep 2026, Lean-formalized but unreviewed by experts) -> 186 (OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, dated to a paper released with the model on/around 3 Sep 2026, Lean formalization conditional on three unproven Lean axioms). None of these post-Stadlmann bounds has been digested by an independent human expert as of this writing (22 Sep 2026); the situation is treated by the mathematical community itself as unsettled and contested.

ai.basis_quote: "Announcing that GPT-6 Astra has pushed the prime gap to 186, with Lean formalization!" (OpenAI researcher Weijie Su); the OpenAI paper states the proof 'is due to GPT 6 Astra' and that the improvement combines equidistribution estimates of Polymath 8a and Stadlmann with 'complementary factorization conditions ... and an improved numerical optimization'. Separately, AxiomProver is described by Axiom Math as an 'AI system under development ... [that] autonomously generated from natural-language specifications a Lean certificate' for the H1<=212 result, with the underlying mathematics credited to named human co-authors (Charton, Hong, Lau, Ono, and others). Shiva Kintali stated on X: 'I showed that H1 <= 236 with the help of AI, building on Julia Stadlmann's work,' without naming the model or describing the division of labor.

disputes.summary: In the space of about four days (31 Aug - 3 Sep 2026), four different bound-improvement claims (240, 236, 212, 186) were announced by different parties (a human mathematician, an individual claiming AI-assisted work with no preprint, an AI startup's theorem-proving system, and OpenAI's flagship model), each explicitly building on the previous. The exact chronological ordering of the 212 (Axiom) and 186 (OpenAI) results is unclear from secondary sources: one search summary places OpenAI's preprint date as 30 Aug (before Axiom's 3 Sep announcement) while the Lean development for 186 appears to have posted around 2 Sep, and OpenAI's own framing ties the 186 announcement to the GPT-6 Astra model release event on/around 3 Sep. None of the AI-derived bounds (236, 212, 186) has yet been reviewed or endorsed on the record by an independent human expert not affiliated with the producing organization.

Experts publicly criticized the AI-driven race as harmful to the field even where the results are not in mathematical dispute. Andrew Granville said OpenAI should have contacted Stadlmann directly rather than only her advisor Kevin Ford; Ford worried the dynamic could discourage young researchers; Terence Tao criticized prioritizing benchmark numbers over human mathematical understanding. Number theorist Thomas Bloom explicitly flagged Stadlmann's 240 result as notable specifically for being '(by a human!)', implying the subsequent bounds were viewed differently by the community.

summary: This bullet (a nested sub-case of Landau's problems) asks whether there are infinitely many twin primes. That remains completely open: no source claims to have proven or disproven it. What did happen in the window is the Wikipedia article's own headline auxiliary fact — the best known unconditional value of H1 = liminf(p_{n+1}-p_n), the smallest gap proven to recur infinitely often (2 iff the conjecture holds) — moved for the first time since 2014, and moved four times in about four days. Julia Stadlmann (arXiv:2608.31126, submitted 31 Aug 2026), working alone with traditional methods and no AI, proved H1 <= 240, improving the Polymath8b/Maynard bound of 246 that had stood since 2014; this is squarely 'progress' on a record-type sub-question, confirmed by expert reaction (Granville, Soundararajan, Bloom all publicly praised it as a genuine, human-authored advance) even though it has not yet gone through full peer review, so I treat it as the anchor human result. Within days, Shiva Kintali announced H1<=236 'with the help of AI' on X with no preprint, no named model, and no review (VibeMathed logs it as an unreviewed, thin claim). Axiom Math's AxiomProver system then produced H1<=212, credited to named human co-authors (Charton, Hong, Lau, Ono, et al.) with the AI system generating the Lean formalization/certificate from natural-language specification — per Axiom's own site this is a case where the mathematics is attributed to the humans and the AI's contribution is described as formalization, though the underlying mathematical derivation process is not fully disclosed either. Almost simultaneously, OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra had reached H1<=186, with OpenAI's own paper stating the proof 'is due to GPT-6 Astra' — the strongest authorial claim of AI-generated mathematics among the four bounds — but the accompanying Lean formalization is explicitly conditional on three unproven axioms (two Kloosterman-sum bounds from Deligne/Fouvry-Kowalski-Michel, cited but not formalized, plus numerically-verified-but-unproven integral bounds), and by the Hacker News discussion's own characterization, 'the proof file is roughly 10MB of Lean with no independent human semantic review yet.' None of the three post-Stadlmann bounds (236, 212, 186) meets this dataset's bar for `resolved` (expert digestion) or arguably even stable `claimed` status, since the whole sequence is still shifting and disputed; I classify the overall event as `progress` (an instructive, ongoing incident on a still-open problem) and set ai_role to `bound` because, taking the clearest and best-documented AI claim (OpenAI/GPT-6 Astra), an AI system is credited by its own developers with moving an unconditional-looking (but formally conditional) numerical bound on a problem that remains open — this is exactly the `bound` category's definition, not `generated` (which would require a settled result, and this is a live-record contest, not a resolution) and not `assisted` (Axiom's account attributes the mathematics to humans). I could not find a single authoritative source resolving the exact chronological order of the 212 and 186 claims, or any expert consensus on which (if any) is currently considered the valid record; multiple sources call the whole episode unresolved/contested as of writing.
competing_reading: One could argue this record-chasing episode is entirely a 'related' quantity (H1, a bound on gaps) rather than a case of the twin prime conjecture itself, and that per SS3.1's rule that record-table extensions on an infinitude question ('are there infinitely many X') don't count unless the record is the question, this whole event should be `open`/`no_change_found`. I judge H1 is not a pure record table narrowing search space (like 'largest known twin prime pair') but is the specific auxiliary constant Wikipedia's own article cites as the state of the art on this exact conjecture (DHL[k,2]-type results are the standard proxy for progress toward the conjecture in the literature and on the page itself), so a change in H1 is the kind of bound-movement SS6.1's `progress` category is designed to capture. If a stricter reading is taken, the correct status would be `open` with `no_change_found` true and this entire episode relegated to `summary` as context.
what_would_settle_it: An independent, on-the-record verification (a peer-reviewed paper, a widely-endorsed blog post by a named expert working through the Lean formalization line-by-line, or explicit acceptance by the Polymath-style community) confirming which of the 212 or 186 bounds (or a further one) is the actual current unconditional record, and clarification of whether OpenAI's three unproven Lean axioms have since been discharged.

judgement.doubts: All events are bounds on H1; the bullet (infinitely many twin primes) stays open, so progress is the ceiling. The status rests on the 186 bound, which supersedes 240/236/212 on the same quantity; it is unreviewed and its formal proof is conditional on axioms, so if it failed the row would fall back to Axiom's 212 (ai_role none, formalisation only) or Stadlmann's 240 (none). Record's early 'ai_role bound' rationale is obsolete; the 2026-09-24 correction to generated is right. The 212/186 ordering is unclear but irrelevant since 186 is the stronger bound. Unvetted 2025 full-proof preprints were rightly not counted.
